14337.title: DBSCAN
14337.heading: DBSCAN
14337.content:
DBSCAN is a density-based clustering algorithm that grows clusters from points with sufficiently populated radius neighborhoods. It discovers arbitrarily shaped groups and labels observations outside dense regions as noise.

The algorithm does not require the number of clusters in advance. Its radius, minimum-point threshold, and distance measure must match the data's scale and density structure.

14339.sourceSearchName: dbscan noise point dbscan noise point
14339.title: DBSCAN Noise Point
14339.heading: Document

14340.sourceSearchName: dbscan noise point dbscan noise point
14340.title: DBSCAN Noise Point
14340.heading: DBSCAN Noise Point
14340.content:
A DBSCAN noise point is neither a core point nor a border point under the selected Eps and MinPts parameters. It is left outside the discovered density-connected clusters.

Noise is a model-relative label, not proof of error. Changing the radius, minimum count, metric, or data representation can change the classification.

14341.sourceSearchName: dbscan noise point dbscan noise point
14341.title: DBSCAN Noise Point
14341.heading: References

14342.sourceSearchName: dbscan neighborhood parameters dbscan neighborhood parameters
14342.title: DBSCAN Neighborhood Parameters
14342.heading: Document

14343.sourceSearchName: dbscan neighborhood parameters dbscan neighborhood parameters
14343.title: DBSCAN Neighborhood Parameters
14343.heading: DBSCAN Neighborhood Parameters
14343.content:
DBSCAN uses Eps as the radius around a point and MinPts as the minimum number of observations required for a dense neighborhood. Together they determine which points can initiate cluster growth.

A radius that is too small fragments groups and creates noise; one that is too large merges structures. One global setting can struggle when densities vary.

14344.sourceSearchName: dbscan neighborhood parameters dbscan neighborhood parameters
14344.title: DBSCAN Neighborhood Parameters
14344.heading: References

14345.sourceSearchName: dbscan core point dbscan core point
14345.title: DBSCAN Core Point
14345.heading: Document

14346.sourceSearchName: dbscan core point dbscan core point
14346.title: DBSCAN Core Point
14346.heading: DBSCAN Core Point
14346.content:
A DBSCAN core point has at least MinPts observations inside its Eps neighborhood. It represents a locally dense location from which the algorithm can expand a cluster.

Core points connected through chains of dense neighborhoods belong to the same cluster. Nearby non-core observations may be included as border points.

14347.sourceSearchName: dbscan core point dbscan core point
14347.title: DBSCAN Core Point
14347.heading: References

14348.sourceSearchName: dbscan border point dbscan border point
14348.title: DBSCAN Border Point
14348.heading: Document

14349.sourceSearchName: dbscan border point dbscan border point
14349.title: DBSCAN Border Point
14349.heading: DBSCAN Border Point
14349.content:
A DBSCAN border point has fewer than MinPts observations in its own Eps neighborhood but lies within the neighborhood of a core point. It belongs to a cluster without being able to initiate further dense expansion.

Its assignment can depend on which adjacent cluster reaches it first when dense regions are close.

14352.title: Day-for-Night Compositing
14352.heading: Day-for-Night Compositing
14352.content: Turning a daytime plate into night is more than making the whole image blue and dark. The book separately controls the sky, desaturates and lowers contrast, places gradients where upper structures would receive less light, and shapes color channels toward a night look. It then restores believable local sources: window mattes add warm light and blurred glow, while additional mattes create reflected light pools. Lights should not spill indiscriminately into the sky. The scene must retain a readable hierarchy of darkness and illumination.

14355.sourceSearchName: datum as representation datum as representation
14355.title: Datum as Representation
14355.heading: Datum as Representation
14355.content:
A datum is a recorded representation of some aspect of the world, not the aspect itself. A row may stand for a customer, transaction, or event, but the selected fields capture only the properties that collection systems could observe and that analysts chose to retain.

This distinction matters when interpreting results. A model learns relationships among recorded attributes; omitted circumstances and measurement choices remain outside its view. Treating the dataset as a partial abstraction encourages domain checks before a statistical pattern is converted into a claim about people or causes.

14357.title: Date Parsing
14357.heading: Document
14357.content:
2026-09-06 18:44

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Analytic Data Preparation]] · [[Data Quality and Missing Data]]

14358.title: Date Parsing
14358.heading: Date Parsing
14358.content:
Date parsing converts a character or factor representation into a date class by specifying the order and format of its components. Month names, numeric months, two- or four-digit years, weekday text, and separators all require matching format codes.

A value that looks like a date on screen may still be text internally. Parsing should therefore be followed by a class check and sample comparison, because a mistaken format can produce missing or misinterpreted dates that contaminate every later time calculation.

In the book's wrangling pattern, corrected dates become the basis for [[Derived Temporal Feature|derived year and season features]]. Parsing must precede that derivation so apparently valid text does not produce misleading calendar groups.

14361.title: Date Difference
14361.heading: Date Difference
14361.content:
A date difference is the elapsed time between two parsed dates, often expressed in days. It can measure follow-up from an index event to a reference date or help determine whether a later event falls inside a predefined observation window.

The operation is meaningful only after both operands have valid date classes and a clear temporal interpretation. A fixed calendar censoring date and a subject-specific window, such as sixty days after discharge, answer different questions.

14364.title: Dataveillance
14364.heading: Dataveillance
14364.content:
Dataveillance is surveillance carried out through the collection and analysis of data about people's communications and activities. Digital systems allow governments, corporations, and data brokers to monitor behavior at a scale not possible with isolated paper records.

The practice often works through ordinary transactions and mobile services rather than visible observation. Its power comes from combining records over time to infer identity, habits, relationships, and likely future behavior.

14366.sourceSearchName: dataset structure check dataset structure check
14366.title: Dataset Structure Check
14366.heading: Document
14366.content:
2026-09-06 18:44

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Analytic Data Preparation]] · [[R Data Ingestion and Review]]

14367.sourceSearchName: dataset structure check dataset structure check
14367.title: Dataset Structure Check
14367.heading: Dataset Structure Check
14367.content:
A dataset structure check verifies the shape and schema of data immediately after import. It compares observed row and column counts, names, classes, storage modes, levels, and missingness with the expected metadata.

This check catches silent transformations such as renamed variables, unexpected factor conversion, or a source field read with the wrong type. Later statistical output cannot repair a mismatch introduced at import, so structural validation belongs at the beginning of the pipeline.

The book operationalizes structure review through dimensions, a compact glimpse, first and last records, and random rows. These complementary views expose both schema-wide problems and malformed observations that a single preview might miss.

14368.sourceSearchName: dataset structure check dataset structure check
14368.title: Dataset Structure Check
14368.heading: References

14369.title: Dataset Representativeness
14369.heading: Document
14369.content:
2026-09-05 23:09

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Data Ethics and Digital Power]]

14370.title: Dataset Representativeness
14370.heading: Dataset Representativeness
14370.content:
Dataset representativeness is the degree to which data cover the people, situations, and variation relevant to a model's intended use. Size alone does not guarantee representation. A large collection can systematically omit groups, environments, or rare but consequential cases.

Poor representation makes learned performance uneven and can create [[Algorithmic Bias]]. The appropriate comparison population depends on the deployment context, so a dataset suitable for one task may fail in another. Evaluating representativeness requires examining how examples were produced and selected, not only summary statistics after collection.

14372.sourceSearchName: dataset partition verification dataset partition verification
14372.title: Dataset Partition Verification
14372.heading: Document

14373.sourceSearchName: dataset partition verification dataset partition verification
14373.title: Dataset Partition Verification
14373.heading: Dataset Partition Verification
14373.content:
Dataset partition verification checks that records divided into retained and excluded groups still account for the original dataset. A basic test compares the original row count with the sum of the output partition counts.

This arithmetic invariant detects gaps and overlaps created by incorrect Boolean conditions or missing-value behavior. Passing it does not prove that the substantive criteria are correct, but failing it proves that the split was not implemented as intended.

14374.sourceSearchName: dataset partition verification dataset partition verification
14374.title: Dataset Partition Verification
14374.heading: References

14375.title: Dataset Import
14375.heading: Document
14375.content:
2026-09-06 18:44

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Analytic Data Preparation]] · [[R Data Ingestion and Review]]

14376.title: Dataset Import
14376.heading: Dataset Import
14376.content:
Dataset import converts a stored file into an object that statistical software can analyze. The correct reader depends on the source format, such as CSV, SAS transport, SAS data, SPSS, or Stata, and the imported object should be named without altering the authoritative source file.

Import is not complete when the command runs successfully. The analyst must perform a [[Dataset Structure Check]] to confirm the expected number of observations, columns, names, classes, and missing values before any recoding begins.

In the book's reusable pattern, the selected resource is imported into a generic working object and then checked before any substantive analysis. The resource identity and transformation path remain part of provenance even when a convenient object name is reused.

14378.title: Dataset Glimpse
14378.heading: Document
14378.content:
2026-09-16 00:09

Status: #baby

Tags: [[R Data Ingestion and Review]]

14379.title: Dataset Glimpse
14379.heading: Dataset Glimpse
14379.content:
A dataset glimpse is a compact inspection of a table's dimensions, column names, variable types, and sample values. It helps an analyst spot obvious schema problems without printing the entire dataset.

The book uses this review early in ingestion so character, factor, date, and numeric fields can be corrected before modeling.

14381.sourceSearchName: dataset dimension review dataset dimension review
14381.title: Dataset Dimension Review
14381.heading: Document
14381.content:
2026-09-16 00:09

Status: #baby

Tags: [[R Data Ingestion and Review]]

14382.sourceSearchName: dataset dimension review dataset dimension review
14382.title: Dataset Dimension Review
14382.heading: Dataset Dimension Review
14382.content:
A dataset dimension review checks the number of rows and columns immediately after import. Comparing the observed dimensions with an expected count can expose a wrong delimiter, dropped records, duplicated headers, or an unintended file.

Dimension review is a quick first step before examining classes, names, distributions, and missingness.

14383.sourceSearchName: dataset dimension review dataset dimension review
14383.title: Dataset Dimension Review
14383.heading: References

14384.title: Dataset Abstraction
14384.heading: Document
14384.content:
2026-09-05 23:09

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Data Ethics and Digital Power]]

14385.title: Dataset Abstraction
14385.heading: Dataset Abstraction
14385.content:
Dataset abstraction is the reduction of people, objects, or events to selected variables and records that a model can process. The dataset is a map of reality rather than reality itself: it preserves some distinctions, removes others, and reflects the purpose and methods of its construction.

Treating the abstraction as complete can turn measurement choices into apparently objective facts. A model may be precise about the representation while missing qualities the representation excluded. Ethical data practice therefore asks who defined the categories, what context was lost, and whether the abstraction remains suitable when data are reused for a different decision.

14388.title: DataFrame
14388.heading: DataFrame
14388.content:
A DataFrame is a distributed collection organized into named columns with known structure. The schema gives a query optimizer more semantic information than an opaque collection of application objects.

In Spark SQL, DataFrame operations and relational queries can share an optimized execution plan while remaining connected to the broader Spark runtime.

14390.title: Dataflow Graph
14390.heading: Document
14390.content:
2026-09-06 21:16

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Augmented Reality Software Architecture]] [[Scalable Social Data Processing]]

14391.title: Dataflow Graph
14391.heading: Dataflow Graph
14391.content:
A dataflow graph represents processing components as nodes and their data dependencies as directed connections. A change from a tracker can propagate through transformation, filtering, interaction, and rendering nodes toward a displayed result.

The graph makes the pipeline inspectable and reconfigurable. Cycles, differing update rates, threads, and distributed connections require an execution policy that prevents uncontrolled latency or inconsistent values.

In large-scale data processing, a compiler can translate a high-level script into successive logical and physical dataflow graphs. Operators form the nodes, directed dependencies determine execution order, and optimization rewrites the graph before distributed jobs are generated.

14394.title: Dataflow Architecture
14394.heading: Dataflow Architecture
14394.content:
A dataflow architecture expresses computation as components connected by the movement of data. A source produces measurements, filters transform them, and consumers use the resulting values for simulation, interaction, or rendering.

The structure suits AR pipelines because components can be developed and tested separately, then connected locally or across hosts. Scheduling and buffering must preserve acceptable latency and ensure that data dependencies update coherently.

14397.title: Datafication
14397.heading: Datafication
14397.content:
Datafication transforms activities, relationships, and experiences into quantified records that can be stored and analyzed. Mobile devices accelerate this process by continuously producing location, communication, search, purchase, and application-use data.

Once behavior is represented as data, it can be aggregated for prediction and targeting beyond the immediate service. Datafication therefore expands both the convenience of personalization and the reach of [[Dataveillance]].

14399.sourceSearchName: database first development database first development
14399.title: Database-First Development
14399.heading: Document

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Entity Framework Core Data Modeling]] [[Entity Framework Core Data Access]]

14400.sourceSearchName: database first development database first development
14400.title: Database-First Development
14400.heading: Database-First Development
14400.content:
Database-first development begins with an existing database and derives application entity classes and mappings from its schema. It is useful when the database already exists or is controlled separately from the application code.

Schema changes originate in the database and may require regenerated or updated application mappings. This reverses the direction used by [[Code-First Development]], where entity classes and migrations lead the schema.

For EF Core 3, the book describes database-first as a one-way starting operation: tooling can reverse-engineer a code model from an existing schema, but subsequent database changes are generated from the resulting code model rather than continuously synchronized both ways.

In the database-first approach, the existing tables, columns, and relationships are inspected to generate application model classes. Schema changes originate in the database and require the generated model to be refreshed or regenerated deliberately.

14401.sourceSearchName: database first development database first development
14401.title: Database-First Development

14403.sourceSearchName: database backed cms import database backed cms import
14403.title: Database-Backed CMS Import
14403.heading: Database-Backed CMS Import
14403.content:
A database-backed CMS import maps existing records into the content types, identifiers, and relationships expected by the new system. It must preserve meaning while translating source fields into structured pages, posts, components, or media references.

Reliable imports are repeatable, validated, and explicit about conflicts and missing data. Running them as a controlled migration is safer than embedding one-time assumptions in ordinary request handling.

14406.sourceSearchName: database round trip database round trip
14406.title: Database Round Trip
14406.heading: Database Round Trip
14406.content:
A database round trip is one request-response exchange between the application and its database. Each trip includes more than query execution: a connection path, command transfer, result transfer, and application-side processing all contribute latency.

Repeated queries inside a loop can make round trips grow with the number of parent records. Combining related work through joins or multiple result sets can reduce that cost when the resulting query and mapping remain manageable.

14408.title: Database Seeding
14408.heading: Document
14408.content:

14409.title: Database Seeding
14409.heading: Database Seeding
14409.content:
Database seeding populates a database with an initial or known set of records after its structure is available. Seed data can establish application prerequisites, development examples, or default identities and roles.

The WorldCities application imports city and country data through a seed controller, while its identity setup creates default users and roles. Seeding should be repeatable enough to avoid creating unintended duplicates when it runs again.

14412.title: Database Migration
14412.heading: Database Migration
14412.content:
A database migration is an ordered, repeatable change that advances a database schema or required data from one version to the next. Applied migrations are journaled so the same change is not executed again on a later startup.

Migration scripts allow the database and application to evolve together. They should be additive and reviewable enough that deployment can determine what will change before the new application depends on it.

14414.title: Database Context
14414.heading: Document
14414.content:
2026-09-06 20:34

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Entity Framework Core Data Modeling]]

14415.title: Database Context
14415.heading: Database Context
14415.content:
A database context is the Entity Framework Core object that represents a session with the database and coordinates entity sets, mappings, queries, and saved changes. An application-specific context declares the entities that belong to its model.

The context is configured with a database provider and connection information, then supplied to controllers or services through [[Dependency Injection]]. Tests can replace the production configuration with an [[In-Memory Database Provider]].

14417.sourceSearchName: database as a service database as a service
14417.title: Database as a Service
14417.heading: Document

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Service and Deployment Models]]

14418.sourceSearchName: database as a service database as a service
14418.title: Database as a Service
14418.heading: Database as a Service
14418.content:
Database as a service provides an accessible database system as a reusable cloud capability. The provider supplies the platform and storage beneath it, while applications connect through established query languages and connectivity protocols.

Keeping the database near the applications that use it can reduce transaction delay. A standardized database service can also be instantiated as a reusable [[Cloud Cell]], but licensing, performance, data protection, and the ability to move data remain important constraints.

14421.sourceSearchName: data to knowledge transformation data to knowledge transformation
14421.title: Data-to-Knowledge Transformation
14421.heading: Data-to-Knowledge Transformation
14421.content:
Data-to-knowledge transformation is the progression from recorded observations to structured information, interpreted patterns, and actionable understanding. Each stage adds context and judgment rather than simply increasing the amount of data.

The book uses this progression to explain why cleaning, exploration, modeling, validation, and communication are all parts of [[Data Science]].

14422.sourceSearchName: data to knowledge transformation data to knowledge transformation

14423.title: Data-Oriented Middleware
14423.heading: Document

14424.sourceSearchName: data oriented middleware data oriented middleware
14424.title: Data-Oriented Middleware
14424.heading: Data-Oriented Middleware
14424.content:
Data-oriented middleware lets applications share persistent datasets through a database or comparable data service. The shared store becomes an integration point at which independently implemented applications can query and update agreed records.

Connectivity protocols and query languages can make the store accessible across platforms. A [[Common Data Model]], transaction rules, ownership, and concurrency behavior are still needed so shared access does not create inconsistent meanings or updates.

14427.sourceSearchName: data driven ui add on data driven ui add on
14427.title: Data-Driven UI Add-On
14427.heading: Data-Driven UI Add-On
14427.content:
A data-driven UI add-on combines script behavior with declarative data files so users or content authors can extend a game's interface without changing the engine. The files describe layout and metadata, while scripts respond to events and update elements.

Powerful extension points require a security boundary. Privileged operations can remain in protected engine code, with add-ons permitted to observe or hook approved behavior rather than replace core functions.

14429.sourceSearchName: data driven inductivism data driven inductivism
14429.title: Data-Driven Inductivism
14429.heading: Document

14430.sourceSearchName: data driven inductivism data driven inductivism
14430.title: Data-Driven Inductivism
14430.heading: Data-Driven Inductivism
14430.content:
Data-driven inductivism is the view that general patterns, predictions, or causal claims can be developed from observations with relatively little prior theory. Data science renews this position by making very large collections and powerful pattern detection available.

The view does not imply that data interpret themselves. The source argues that a defensible inductivism needs methods for distinguishing useful causal structure from accidental correlation and for improving claims as further evidence arrives.

14431.sourceSearchName: data driven inductivism data driven inductivism
14431.title: Data-Driven Inductivism
14431.heading: References

14432.sourceSearchName: data driven design data driven design
14432.title: Data-Driven Design
14432.heading: Document

14433.sourceSearchName: data driven design data driven design
14433.title: Data-Driven Design
14433.heading: Data-Driven Design
14433.content:
Data-driven design stores part definitions, attributes, and values separately from program code, often in a spreadsheet exported to a machine-readable format. The game loads those values over safe defaults at runtime.

This separation lets designers tune and balance content without changing code or waiting for a full rebuild. Hot reloading shortens the [[Designer Loop]], provided the design documents, data, and implemented structures remain synchronized.

14434.sourceSearchName: data driven design data driven design
14434.title: Data-Driven Design
14434.heading: References

14436.title: Data Transformation
14436.heading: Data Transformation
14436.content:
Data transformation converts extracted records into forms that can be combined and analyzed. It can standardize types, units, formats, categories, or structures and derive fields needed by later processing.

A transformation should make its semantic assumptions explicit. Two values that look compatible after conversion may still represent different events or populations, so technical uniformity does not guarantee conceptual equivalence.

14438.sourceSearchName: data driven culture data driven culture
14438.title: Data-Driven Culture
14438.heading: Document

14439.sourceSearchName: data driven culture data driven culture
14439.title: Data-Driven Culture
14439.heading: Data-Driven Culture
14439.content:
A data-driven culture expects claims and organizational choices to be informed by accessible evidence. It combines technical capability with routines for asking questions, challenging assumptions, sharing results, and revising action.

Culture matters because an accurate analysis has little effect if it is isolated from authority and workflow. Evidence must be understandable, timely, and connected to the people who can act on it.

14440.sourceSearchName: data driven culture data driven culture
14440.title: Data-Driven Culture
14440.heading: References

14441.title: Data Warehousing
14441.heading: Document
14441.content:
2026-09-09 03:12

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Data Mining Process and Infrastructure]]

14442.title: Data Warehousing
14442.heading: Data Warehousing
14442.content:
Data warehousing is the organizational and technical process of creating, maintaining, and using a [[Data Warehouse]]. It integrates disparate databases, organizes large stores by subject, and supports efficient retrieval and interpretation.

Separating decision-support data from operational processing can improve accessibility and analytic consistency. Continued quality controls are needed because integrated data can preserve inconsistencies as easily as it preserves facts.

14444.title: Data Warehouse
14444.heading: Document
14444.content:
2026-09-09 03:12

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Data Mining Process and Infrastructure]]

14445.title: Data Warehouse
14445.heading: Data Warehouse
14445.content:
A data warehouse is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-varying, and generally non-updatable collection designed to support management decisions and business intelligence. It consolidates data from otherwise separate operational sources.

A common, high-quality repository gives data mining a consistent view of organizational history. It does not remove the need to understand provenance, definitions, or changes in source systems.

The book adds that a warehouse can materially shorten individual data science projects because extraction, standardization, and integration have already been done for shared use. Its historic records also allow models to be rolled through earlier time periods and checked for changing accuracy. A central repository is helpful, not a prerequisite for data science.

14447.sourceSearchName: data veracity in law data veracity in law
14447.title: Data Veracity in Law
14447.heading: Document

14448.sourceSearchName: data veracity in law data veracity in law
14448.title: Data Veracity in Law
14448.heading: Data Veracity in Law
14448.content:
Data veracity in law is the reliability and truthfulness required when information supports a legal determination or automated decision. More records do not compensate for uncertainty about their accuracy, provenance, meaning, or completeness.

Veracity is especially important when an analysis is presented as evidence. Decision makers need to know how observations were produced and whether the analytical conclusion remains justified under the applicable evidentiary standard.

14449.sourceSearchName: data veracity in law data veracity in law
14449.title: Data Veracity in Law
14449.heading: References

14450.title: Data Validation
14450.heading: Document
14450.content:
2026-09-06 18:44

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Analytic Data Preparation]] [[Web Forms and Validation]] · [[Data Quality and Missing Data]]

14451.title: Data Validation
14451.heading: Data Validation
14451.content:
Data validation tests whether an edited dataset has the intended values, relationships, and population before analysis. It includes schema checks, recode cross-tabs, partition counts, distribution review, missingness assessment, and bivariate comparisons that may reveal anomalies.

Validation should be encoded in the workflow rather than performed only by visual memory. A dataset can load without errors and still violate its codebook, lose records during subsetting, or contain an impossible relationship between an event and its measurement time.

In a web application, validation also checks form input before it changes persistent state. [[Client-Side Validation]] supplies immediate feedback, while [[Server-Side Validation]] remains authoritative because the browser can be bypassed. Rules that depend on stored values can be evaluated through an [[Asynchronous Validator]].

The book validates imported data by checking dimensions, types, categorical levels, plausible values, missingness, and the target. These tests turn cleaning into an auditable sequence rather than a collection of silent corrections.

14453.sourceSearchName: data value externality data value externality
14453.title: Data Value Externality
14453.heading: Document
14453.content:
2026-09-17 09:48

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Data Ownership and Access Rights]]

14454.sourceSearchName: data value externality data value externality
14454.title: Data Value Externality
14454.heading: Data Value Externality
14454.content:
A data value externality occurs when an organization captures benefits from data while shifting some costs or risks to people who generated, supplied, or are represented by it. Privacy loss, unfair profiling, and weakened bargaining power may remain outside the firm's price calculation.

Recognizing the externality explains why possession alone may not justify unrestricted use. Liability, access rights, compensation, or governance duties can be considered alongside ownership.

14455.title: Data Value Externality
14455.heading: References

14457.title: Data Type and Permissible Operations
14457.heading: Data Type and Permissible Operations
14457.content:
An attribute's measurement type constrains sensible arithmetic and comparison. Nominal values distinguish categories without order; ordinal values have an order but not necessarily equal distances; numeric interval values admit meaningful differences, while ratio values also have a meaningful zero and ratios.

Encoding categories as numbers does not make their numeric distances real. A model or transformation that averages arbitrary category codes can introduce relationships absent from the domain. Choosing a data representation therefore includes checking what operations the values actually justify.

14460.sourceSearchName: data transfer object data transfer object
14460.title: Data Transfer Object
14460.heading: Data Transfer Object
14460.content:
A data transfer object is a class shaped specifically for data sent across an application boundary. It can include values required by the client while omitting entity properties that should not be serialized or exposed.

Using a DTO preserves [[Separation of Concerns]] between persistence and presentation. It also gives tests a named, typed result, whereas a quick projection to an anonymous type is less reusable outside the method that created it.

In a domain-centered application, request DTOs form the [[Public API Contract]] rather than becoming domain objects. They favor serialization-friendly primitive values and carry data across the transport boundary; the [[Application Layer]] converts them into an [[Application Command]] or domain-specific values before invoking behavior. This prevents HTTP and serializer requirements from leaking into the [[Domain Model]].

14463.title: Data Transaction Costs
14463.heading: Data Transaction Costs
14463.content:
Data transaction costs are the resources required to find relevant data, identify a rights holder, evaluate quality and permission, negotiate terms, and enforce an agreement. These costs can prevent beneficial exchange even when both sides would gain.

Standardized property forms can reduce some uncertainty, but creating new exclusive rights can also multiply the permissions that must be cleared. The design question is whether a rule lowers coordination costs across the whole market.

14466.title: Data Technician
14466.heading: Data Technician
14466.content:
A data technician prepares the foundations of analysis by acquiring, storing, cleaning, and organizing data. Reliable technical handling matters because errors in formats, types, or provenance can invalidate every later model.

This role anchors the first stage in the book's progression from raw data through analysis and mining to data science.

14469.title: Data Science
14469.heading: Data Science
14469.content:
Data science is the disciplined transformation of data into information and usable knowledge. It joins statistical analysis, computation, domain judgment, communication, and repeatable workflows rather than treating an algorithm as the whole practice.

The book frames this work as an end-to-end process: obtain and clean data, explore it, build and validate models, and communicate findings in a form that others can reproduce.

14472.title: Data Subject
14472.heading: Data Subject
14472.content:
A data subject is the person to whom [[Personal Data]] relates. The concept ties information-processing duties to an individual even when the dataset uses an indirect identifier rather than a name.

In large combined datasets, identifying the subject can be uncertain because records may be linked or reattributed later. Rights and safeguards therefore depend on realistic possibilities of identification, not only on the label attached to a field.

14475.title: Data Stream Compression
14475.heading: Data Stream Compression
14475.content:
Data stream compression reduces the number of bits transmitted or stored for a continuing sequence. Sensor streams often contain temporal correlation and repeated values that can be encoded as changes, summaries, or models rather than raw samples.

Lossless methods preserve exact recovery; lossy methods trade accuracy for stronger reduction. The acceptable error depends on the later decision, not only the compression ratio.

14478.title: Data Stratification
14478.heading: Data Stratification
14478.content:
Data stratification divides observations into groups defined by the value or range of another variable and examines the outcome distribution within each group. It can reveal how a relationship changes across a predictor instead of reducing all observations to one aggregate summary.

In the source's height example, grouping sons by rounded father height makes conditional averages and distributions visible. Poorly chosen or sparse strata can introduce noise, so the grouping scale needs substantive and statistical justification.

14481.title: Data Sovereignty
14481.heading: Data Sovereignty
14481.content:
Data sovereignty concerns which party owns data and which legal authority governs that ownership and use. The question becomes difficult when creators, processors, consumers, storage systems, and service providers reside in different countries.

A cloud contract should state ownership, permitted processing, storage location, and the jurisdiction for resolving a breach. Transforming or augmenting data can add contributors without automatically settling who controls the resulting information.

14484.sourceSearchName: data source reconciliation data source reconciliation
14484.title: Data Source Reconciliation
14484.heading: Data Source Reconciliation
14484.content:
Reconciliation resolves differences among sources before their records are treated as one dataset. Customer or patient systems may use different identifiers, units, rating scales, text encodings, or definitions for the same apparent field. Merely copying their tables into one repository does not produce a trustworthy common view.

An analyst must decide which record is authoritative, map alternate representations to agreed values, and investigate ambiguous matches. The work is partly technical and partly semantic: a standardized field is useful only when its meaning remains comparable across sources.

14487.title: Data Sorting
14487.heading: Data Sorting
14487.content:
Data sorting arranges query results by a selected field and direction. In a paged Web API, sorting must occur before the requested page is selected or records can appear in inconsistent positions between pages.

An Angular Material sort control can send the selected column and direction to the server. The server should accept only recognized fields rather than inserting arbitrary client text into a [[Dynamic LINQ]] expression.

14490.title: Data Service
14490.heading: Data Service
14490.content:
A data service centralizes client operations that exchange data with a back-end API. Instead of letting several components call [[Angular HttpClient]] directly, it provides named methods for getting, creating, and updating application records.

The layer creates one place for URL construction, response typing, post-processing, error handling, and retries. Domain-specific services can extend a typed base service while components depend on their narrower interfaces.

14493.title: Data Security States
14493.heading: Data Security States
14493.content:
Data protection must cover three operational states: [[Data at Rest]] in storage, [[Data in Transit]] between locations, and [[Data in Process]] while a system uses it. A control that protects only one state leaves transition points or active processing exposed.

Treating the states separately helps designers choose appropriate access, encryption, integrity, and monitoring controls for the way information exists at each moment.

14496.title: Data Scientist
14496.heading: Data Scientist
14496.content:
A data scientist combines statistical reasoning, machine learning, software practice, and domain understanding to turn data into decisions. The role extends beyond producing a model because the scientist must also test assumptions, explain uncertainty, and make the analysis repeatable.

The book presents the role as a progression from data handling and analysis toward discovering patterns and creating new knowledge.

14499.sourceSearchName: data science project sponsorship data science project sponsorship
14499.title: Data Science Project Sponsorship
14499.heading: Data Science Project Sponsorship
14499.content:
Project sponsorship gives a data science effort an organizational owner who cares about the business process and use of its results. The book emphasizes support from senior business management, not simply an IT mandate to keep systems operational.

A sponsor can define the decision to improve, secure cooperation across domain and technical teams, and support repeated use after the first demonstration. Treating data science as a one-off box-ticking exercise leaves even an accurate model without a durable pathway to value.

14502.sourceSearchName: data science problem framing data science problem framing
14502.title: Data Science Problem Framing
14502.heading: Data Science Problem Framing
14502.content:
Problem framing translates a real-world goal into a task whose required evidence and output can be specified. The book identifies clustering, anomaly detection, association-rule mining, and prediction as four common task classes. Prediction further divides into categorical classification and numeric regression.

Choosing the task early changes dataset design. A churn classifier needs historic cases with churn labels; a clustering study does not require a target attribute. The business-understanding phase should therefore specify both the intended action and the kind of pattern that could inform it before selecting an algorithm.

14505.sourceSearchName: data science pipeline data science pipeline
14505.title: Data Science Pipeline
14505.heading: Data Science Pipeline
14505.content:
A data science pipeline is the sequence through which data are captured, cleaned, combined, selected, restructured, modeled, interpreted, and used for action. Ethical choices occur at every stage, not only when a finished model produces a decision.

Collection determines who becomes visible. Cleaning and selection decide which records count as errors or relevant evidence. Modeling chooses a target and a representation, while interpretation connects a statistical pattern to a real-world judgment. Because responsibility is distributed across this sequence, documenting transformations and decisions supports [[AI Traceability]] and makes hidden assumptions easier to challenge.

The book's CRISP-DM account makes the sequence iterative. Business understanding, data understanding, preparation, modeling, evaluation, and deployment can send work back to an earlier decision when data quality, model behavior, or practical usefulness falls short. The pipeline ends in a decision process and its monitoring, not in a model file.

14508.sourceSearchName: data science capability data science capability
14508.title: Data Science Capability
14508.heading: Data Science Capability
14508.content:
Data science capability is the combined organizational ability to obtain data, use appropriate tools, apply analytic judgment, and deliver reproducible knowledge. It depends on people, process, infrastructure, and governance rather than on software alone.

Capability grows when exploratory work can progress into validated models and clear reports without losing provenance or repeatability.

14510.title: Data Repurposing

14511.title: Data Repurposing
14511.heading: Data Repurposing
14511.content:
Data repurposing occurs when information collected for one purpose is later used for another. Combining records can reveal sensitive patterns or support decisions that the person could not reasonably anticipate when the information was first provided.

Repurposing weakens consent when permission for the original context is treated as permission for every future analysis. It can also create a chilling effect: people alter ordinary behavior because they cannot know how their traces may be interpreted later. [[Privacy by Design]] therefore considers limits on purpose, retention, access, and combination throughout a system's life.

14514.title: Data Repository
14514.heading: Data Repository
14514.content:
A data repository is a concrete service that implements a set of persistence operations for an application. Its methods translate meaningful requests, such as retrieving a question or saving an answer, into database commands.

The repository keeps data-access details out of controllers and can be registered through dependency injection. Its method boundaries also expose where asynchronous execution and transaction decisions belong.

14517.title: Data Replication
14517.heading: Data Replication
14517.content:
Data replication stores copies of information on multiple hosts so one departure or failure does not make the data unavailable. Replicas can also place frequently used content nearer to computation.

More copies improve resilience but consume capacity and network bandwidth. Updates require a consistency rule that defines which versions readers may observe.

14519.title: Data Reidentification

14520.title: Data Reidentification
14520.heading: Data Reidentification
14520.content:
Data reidentification is the process of connecting records that were treated as anonymous back to an identifiable person. Linkage with auxiliary datasets, rare combinations of attributes, or recognizable behavioral patterns can restore an identity without a direct name.

Reidentification makes anonymity a matter of degree and context. A release must be evaluated against the other information and analytical capabilities likely to be available, not only against identifiers removed from the released table.
links: Big Data Law and Individual Rights

14523.title: Data Record
14523.heading: Data Record
14523.content:
A data record is a group of related fields describing one entity for an application. An email record, for example, can contain its sender, delivery date, subject, and message body.

A [[Sorting Algorithm]] reorders whole records according to selected fields called a [[Sort Key]]. The remaining fields travel with the record, so sorting changes position without altering the information represented by each entity.

14525.title: Data Quality
14525.heading: Document

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Big Data Governance and Quality]] · [[Cluster Data Quality and Interpretation]] · [[Evidence-Based Data Decisions]]

14526.title: Data Quality
14526.heading: Data Quality
14526.content:
Data quality is the fitness of data for the decision or analysis it supports. Accuracy, relevance, completeness, consistency, timeliness, and adequate context determine whether a large collection can produce useful conclusions.

Volume does not compensate for poor quality. Errors and irrelevant observations can be amplified by aggregation, while uncertain provenance makes it difficult to explain or correct an outcome.

For cluster analysis, quality is inseparable from representation. Unrelated features distort proximity, incompatible data types can invalidate a method, and stale domains or unenforced business rules can corrupt results. The source emphasizes accuracy, reliability, timeliness, relevance, and completeness as complementary dimensions maintained through ongoing cleansing.

For evidence-based decisions, quality also connects the processing pipeline to the decision context. Veracity, provenance, and adequate cleaning determine whether a pattern can be treated as credible evidence rather than merely as a computable result.

14528.title: Data Protection Transparency

14529.sourceSearchName: data protection transparency data protection transparency
14529.title: Data Protection Transparency
14529.heading: Data Protection Transparency
14529.content:
Data protection transparency requires an organization to make its collection and use of [[Personal Data]] understandable to the people concerned. Meaningful notice identifies the responsible party, purposes, categories of data, important recipients, and ways to exercise rights.

Big-data reuse makes transparency difficult because later combinations and inferences may not be predictable at collection time. That uncertainty is a reason to document evolving purposes, not a reason to abandon explanation.

14532.sourceSearchName: data protection in ai data protection in ai
14532.title: Data Protection in AI
14532.heading: Data Protection in AI
14532.content:
Data protection in AI is the set of rights and controls governing how personal data are collected, stored, processed, accessed, corrected, and erased. It treats privacy as an enforceable relationship between a data subject and the organization using the data.

Automated decision making adds a need for meaningful information about the logic and likely consequences of processing. Erasure, access, and objection rights can restore some control, while [[Privacy by Design]] builds protection into the system rather than depending only on later complaints. Legal compliance remains a minimum; an allowed use can still be manipulative or unjust.

14535.title: Data Protection Accountability
14535.heading: Data Protection Accountability
14535.content:
Data protection accountability makes an organization responsible for both following governing principles and being able to demonstrate that it has done so. Policies must be connected to records of decisions, assigned roles, controls, reviews, and evidence of operation.

For big-data projects, accountability follows the full pipeline from collection and combination through model use, sharing, retention, and deletion.

14538.title: Data Protection Impact Assessment
14538.heading: Data Protection Impact Assessment
14538.content:
A data protection impact assessment examines a proposed processing operation before or during deployment to identify effects on people, justify the purpose, and select safeguards. It treats privacy risk as a property of the complete system rather than of isolated fields.

For large-scale analytics, the assessment must include linkage, inference, opaque processing, secondary uses, and the possibility of group-level harm. It complements individual notice when affected people cannot foresee every later analytical use.

14541.title: Data Parallelism
14541.heading: Data Parallelism
14541.content:
Data parallelism gives multiple workers copies of a model and different subsets of the input. Each worker calculates partial results or gradients, which are then combined to keep the model replicas consistent.

The approach scales when example-level work dominates aggregation. Synchronization and communication can become bottlenecks as worker count grows or updates become more frequent.

14544.title: Data Processing Legitimacy
14544.heading: Data Processing Legitimacy
14544.content:
Data processing legitimacy asks whether an organization has a defensible basis for collecting and using personal data. It is distinct from technical feasibility: the ability to combine or analyze records does not itself authorize that operation.

Legitimacy must be considered together with [[Purpose Limitation]], proportionality, transparency, and the rights of the affected person.

14547.title: Data Privacy
14547.heading: Data Privacy
14547.content:
Data privacy governs information that identifies or can be linked to a person and the conditions under which it may be collected, used, retained, disclosed, or destroyed. It asks not only whether data is secure but whether a party should possess or use it for a particular purpose.

Cloud services complicate privacy because providers, employees, applications, devices, and governments can occupy different legal jurisdictions. Encryption and access controls help protect data, while retention, anonymization, ownership, and lawful use require policy and contractual decisions.

14550.sourceSearchName: data ownership scope data ownership scope
14550.title: Data Ownership Scope
14550.heading: Data Ownership Scope
14550.content:
Data ownership scope specifies the powers, limits, duration, subject matter, and parties bound by a proposed data right. A right might cover access, copying, transfer, commercial use, alteration, or remedies without granting every power associated with physical property.

Scope must also address whether the right sits on top of existing law or replaces other protections. Overbroad exclusivity can obstruct reuse, while a narrow right may fail to correct the problem offered as its justification.

14553.sourceSearchName: data ownership right data ownership right
14553.title: Data Ownership Right
14553.heading: Data Ownership Right
14553.content:
A data ownership right would give a person or organization property-like control over data, potentially including powers to exclude others, transfer access, or seek remedies against interference. The source finds no general, specific property right in data under the Swiss and European rules it examines.

The term is still useful in a broader sense because control can arise through contracts, confidentiality, intellectual-property rules, tort remedies, or technical access. Each mechanism supplies different powers and binds different parties.

14556.sourceSearchName: data ownership attribution data ownership attribution
14556.title: Data Ownership Attribution
14556.heading: Data Ownership Attribution
14556.content:
Data ownership attribution is the rule used to decide who would receive a property-like claim in data. Possible candidates include the person described, the collector, the creator of a database, the party that invested labor or money, or a group whose information produced the value.

Different criteria reward different contributions and can conflict when several parties participate. Attribution must therefore be justified explicitly rather than inferred automatically from physical possession or technical control.

14557.title: Data Ownership Attribution

14559.title: Data Overload
14559.heading: Data Overload
14559.content:
Data overload occurs when a visualization presents more information than a viewer can effectively perceive, organize, or use. In AR, the physical scene is already information-rich, so every annotation competes with real objects and other augmentations.

Cluttered content can obscure the task and impair understanding even when every individual item is relevant. Spatial and knowledge-based filtering, layout, and interaction should control what appears for the current user, location, and purpose.

14562.title: Data Mining
14562.heading: Data Mining
14562.content:
Data mining applies algorithms from statistics, computer science, and machine learning to extract useful patterns from large data collections. Outputs can include classifications, clusters, associations, sequences, correlations, trends, and predictive models.

The algorithmic search is one stage within [[Knowledge Discovery in Databases]]. A pattern becomes useful knowledge only after it is checked for relevance and validity and connected to the goals and practices of its domain.

14565.title: Data Mining Process
14565.heading: Data Mining Process
14565.content:
A compact data mining process defines the problem, prepares and explores the data, selects or constructs a model, explores and validates that model, and deploys and updates it.

These activities are interdependent. Deployment creates new data and feedback, while model exploration can reveal preparation defects. Treating the process as a cycle makes revision part of normal operation.

14568.title: Data Mining Deployment
14568.heading: Data Mining Deployment
14568.content:
Data mining deployment turns an evaluated pattern or model into a maintained part of an information or decision system. It includes a deployment plan, monitoring and maintenance, reporting, and review of the discovery process.

Deployment also exposes models to changing data and business rules. Updating and revalidation are therefore continuing responsibilities rather than one-time implementation tasks.

14571.title: Data Minimization
14571.heading: Data Minimization
14571.content:
Data minimization limits collection and retention to information that is adequate, relevant, and no more extensive than the stated purpose requires. It works with [[Purpose Limitation]] by restricting both what enters a system and what remains available for later processing.

Big-data practices strain this principle because future value is often unknown at collection time. The possibility that additional data might reveal a correlation is not by itself a justification for unlimited accumulation.

14574.title: Data Miner
14574.heading: Data Miner
14574.content:
A data miner searches prepared datasets for predictive or descriptive patterns using statistical and machine-learning methods. The role must distinguish stable structure from artifacts of a particular sample through independent validation.

The book positions data mining between conventional analysis and the broader synthesis expected of a [[Data Scientist]].

14577.title: Data Mart
14577.heading: Data Mart
14577.content:
A data mart is a subset of enterprise data restricted to a particular subject area. It uses a consistent model and makes a focused collection available for efficient analysis.

A mart can reduce the amount of data scanned for a specific mining problem, but its narrower scope may omit relationships visible in the wider warehouse. Its boundaries should follow the analytical question rather than departmental convenience alone.

14580.title: Data Market Failure
14580.heading: Data Market Failure
14580.content:
Data market failure occurs when ordinary exchange does not produce socially useful creation, access, or use of data. Proposed causes include uncertainty about value, weak bargaining positions, externalized costs, and difficulty excluding or coordinating users.

A new ownership right is only one possible response. Regulation, contracts, access duties, liability, standards, or collective arrangements may address a particular failure with different effects on innovation and reuse.

14583.title: Data Loss Prevention
14583.heading: Data Loss Prevention
14583.content:
Data loss prevention is the coordinated discovery, identification, monitoring, management, and protection of sensitive data throughout its life cycle. Its scope includes creation, transmission, active use, storage, backup, archival, retention, and destruction.

Controls must cover [[Data at Rest]], [[Data in Motion]], and [[Data in Use]]. Encryption protects contents, checksums help verify integrity, monitoring records access, and retention management removes stale data when it should no longer be held.

14586.title: Data Locality
14586.heading: Data Locality
14586.content:
Data locality places computation on or near the machine that stores its input. In MapReduce systems, a local map task reads from a worker's disk instead of consuming cluster-network bandwidth.

Waiting indefinitely for a local slot can delay completion, so a scheduler balances locality against queue time, fairness, deadlines, and the distribution of replicas.

14589.title: Data Loading
14589.heading: Data Loading
14589.content:
Data loading writes transformed information into the storage system used for integration, exploration, and analysis. It completes the familiar extraction-transformation-loading path but may occur repeatedly as new data arrive.

Loading design affects timeliness, recoverability, and traceability. A pipeline needs to distinguish successful records, rejected records, and repeated updates so decision makers know which evidence was available at a given time.

14592.sourceSearchName: data link layer data link layer
14592.title: Data Link Layer
14592.heading: Data Link Layer
14592.content:
The data link layer organizes transmission between nodes that share a physical network segment. It frames bits into transferable units, associates them with link-level addresses, and commonly supplies local error detection.

Its scope is one link rather than an end-to-end internet route. The network layer can move a packet across several such links while each data-link implementation handles its immediate medium.
